claim: Two-photon calcium imaging combined with two-photon microscopy has proved useful for monitoring neuronal activity in vivo because of its high selectivity, good signal-to-noise ratio, and depth penetration in scattering tissues.
source: For reading out neuronal activity in vivo, the combination of calcium imaging of neuronal populations (Yuste and Katz, 1991) with two-photon microscopy (Denk et al., 1990), has proved its utility because of its high selectivity, good signal-to-noise ratio, and depth penetration in scattering tissues (Yuste and Denk, 1995; Cossart et al., 2003; Zipfel et al., 2003; Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Svoboda and Yasuda, 2006; Ji et al., 2016; Yang and Yuste, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the utility of this technique.

claim: Two-photon imaging can be combined with two-photon optochemistry or two-photon optogenetics to allow simultaneous readout and manipulation of neural activity with cellular resolution.
source: Moreover, two-photon imaging can be combined with two-photon optochemistry (Nikolenko et al., 2007; Dal Maschio et al., 2010) or two-photon optogenetics (Packer et al., 2012; Rickgauer et al., 2014; Packer et al., 2015; Emiliani et al., 2015; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016) to allow simultaneous readout and manipulation of neural activity with cellular resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating these combined approaches.

claim: Combinations of optical methods into an all-optical approach have been largely restricted to two-dimensional (2D) planes.
source: But so far, the combinations of these optical methods into an all-optical approach have been largely restricted to two-dimensional (2D) planes (Nikolenko et al., 2007; Dal Maschio et al., 2010; Rickgauer et al., 2014; Packer et al., 2015; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work that was limited to 2D.

claim: Neural circuits are three dimensional, and neuronal sub-populations are distributed throughout their volume.
source: At the same time, neural circuits are three dimensional, and neuronal sub-populations are distributed throughout their volume.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of neural circuits.

claim: Extending optical methods to three dimensions (3D) appears essential to enable systematic studies of microcircuit computation and processing.
source: Therefore, extending these methods to three dimensions (3D) appears essential to enable systematic studies of microcircuit computation and processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 3D nature of neural circuits and the limitations of 2D methods.

claim: The authors employed wavefront shaping strategies with a customized dual-beam two-photon microscope to simultaneously perform volumetric calcium imaging and 3D patterned photostimulations in mouse cortex in vivo.
source: Here we employed wavefront shaping strategies with a customized dual-beam two-photon microscope to simultaneously perform volumetric calcium imaging and 3D patterned photostimulations in mouse cortex in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The authors adopted a hybrid strategy that combines 3D holograms and galvanometer driven spiral scans for photostimulation.
source: For phostostimulation, we adopted a hybrid strategy that combines 3D holograms and galvanometer driven spiral scans.
evidence: This describes the specific photostimulation approach used in the study.

claim: The authors used a pulse-amplified low-repetition-rate (200 kHz ~ 1 MHz) laser, which significantly reduces the average laser power required for photoactivation, and minimizes thermal effects and imaging artifacts.
source: Furthermore, we used a pulse-amplified low-repetition-rate (200 kHz ~ 1 MHz) laser, which significantly reduces the average laser power required for photoactivation, and minimizes thermal effects and imaging artifacts.
evidence: This describes the laser system used and its benefits.

claim: The system photostimulated large groups of cells simultaneously in layer 2/3 of primary visual cortex (V1) in awake mice (>80 cells distributed within a 480 × 480 × 150 μm3 imaged volume), while simultaneously imaging the activity of the surrounding neurons.
source: With this system, we photostimulated large groups of cells simultaneously in layer 2/3 of primary visual cortex (V1) in awake mice (>80 cells distributed within a 480 × 480 × 150 μm3 imaged volume), while simultaneously imaging the activity of the surrounding neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental results achieved with the system.

claim: Compared with other 3D all-optical approaches which used scanless holographic photostimulation, the hybrid approach requires less laser power to stimulate per cell, and can thus simultaneously photostimulate more cells for a given fixed power budget.
source: Compared with other 3D all-optical approaches (Dal Maschio et al., 2017; Mardinly et al., 2017), which used scanless holographic photostimulation, our hybrid approach requires less laser power to stimulate per cell, and can thus simultaneously photostimulate more cells for a given fixed power budget.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' approach to prior work, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The all-optical method is useful to analyze the function of neural circuits in 3D, such as studying cell connectivity, ensemble organization, information processing, or excitatory and inhibitory balance.
source: This all-optical method is useful to analyze the function of neural circuits in 3D, such as studying cell connectivity, ensemble organization, information processing, or excitatory and inhibitory balance.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the method.

claim: The authors photostimulated groups of pyramidal cells in 3D with high specificity.
source: As a demonstration, we photostimulated groups of pyramidal cells in 3D with high specificity, and also targeted a selective population of interneurons in V1 in awake mice, finding that stimulating the interneurons reduced the response of pyramidal cells to visual simuli.
evidence: This describes experimental results demonstrating the method's capabilities.

claim: Stimulating interneurons reduced the response of pyramidal cells to visual stimuli in awake mice.
source: As a demonstration, we photostimulated groups of pyramidal cells in 3D with high specificity, and also targeted a selective population of interneurons in V1 in awake mice, finding that stimulating the interneurons reduced the response of pyramidal cells to visual simuli.
evidence: This describes experimental results from the study.

claim: The microscope has two independent two-photon lasers, one for imaging and the other for photostimulation.
source: We built a holographic microscope with two independent two-photon lasers, one for imaging and the other for photostimulation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the microscope design, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Each laser beam's axial focal depth could be controlled without mechanical motion of the objective, yielding maximum flexibility while reducing perturbations to the animal.
source: Each laser beam's axial focal depth could be controlled without mechanical motion of the objective, yielding maximum flexibility while reducing perturbations to the animal.
evidence: This describes a feature of the microscope design.

claim: On the imaging path, a wavelength-tunable Ti:Sapphire laser was coupled through an electrically tunable lens (ETL) followed by a resonant scanner for high speed volumetric imaging.
source: On the imaging path, we coupled a wavelength-tunable Ti:Sapphire laser through an electrically tunable lens (ETL, EL-10-30-C-NIR-LD-MV, Optotune AG) (Grewe et al., 2011) followed by a resonant scanner for high speed volumetric imaging.
evidence: This describes the imaging path configuration.

claim: The ETL, as configured, provided an adjustable axial focus shift up to 90 μm below and 200 μm above the objective's nominal focal plane.
source: The ETL, as configured, provided an adjustable axial focus shift up to 90 μm below and 200 μm above the objective's nominal focal plane.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the ETL in the system.

claim: On the photostimulation path, a low-repetition-rate ultrafast laser was coupled to a spatial light modulator (SLM) to shape the wavefront, allowing flexible 3D beam splitting that simultaneously targets user defined positions in the sample.
source: On the photostimulation path, we used a low-repetition-rate ultrafast laser coupled to a spatial light modulator (SLM, HSP512-1064, Meadowlark Optics) to shape the wavefront, allowing flexible 3D beam splitting that simultaneously targets the user defined positions in the sample (Figure 1B–1E).
evidence: This describes the photostimulation path configuration, supported by Figures 1B-1E.

claim: The axial and lateral targeting error was 0.59 ± 0.54 μm and 0.82 ± 0.65 μm, respectively, across a 3D field of view (FOV) of 240 × 240 × 300 μm3.
source: The axial and lateral targeting error was 0.59 ± 0.54 μm and 0.82 ± 0.65 μm, respectively, across a 3D field of view (FOV) of 240 × 240 × 300 μm3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Materials and Methods).
evidence: This describes the targeting accuracy of the system, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The SLM path was coupled through a pair of standard galvanometers that can allow for fast extension of the targeting FOV beyond that nominal addressable SLM-only range.
source: The SLM path was coupled through a pair of standard galvanometers that can allow for fast extension of the targeting FOV beyond that nominal addressable SLM-only range (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a feature of the photostimulation path, supported by a citation.

claim: For optogenetics experiments, the pair of galvanometric mirrors was actuated to scan the beamlets in a spiral over the cell bodies of the targeted neuron.
source: For optogenetics experiments, we actuated this pair of galvanometric mirrors to scan the beamlets in a spiral over the cell bodies of the targeted neuron (see Figure 1E for an exemplary 3D pattern with 100 targets on an autofluorescent plastic slide).
evidence: This describes the photostimulation approach, supported by Figure 1E.

claim: The approach is termed 'hybrid' as it combined holography with mechanical scanning, as opposed to purely holographic approach.
source: We term this a 'hybrid' approach, as it combined holography with mechanical scanning, as opposed to purely holographic approach.
evidence: This defines the terminology used to describe the approach.

claim: For in vivo experiments, green fluorescence from the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6s or GCaMP6f was imaged and a red-shifted opsin, C1V1-mCherry, was photostimulated.
source: For in vivo experiments, we imaged green fluorescence from the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP6s or GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) and photostimulated a red-shifted opsin, C1V1-mCherry (Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the fluorophores and opsins used in the experiments.

claim: With switchable kinematic mirrors and dichroic mirrors, the lasers could be easily redirected to whichever path, and thus the system could also be utilized for red fluorophores and blue opsins.
source: With switchable kinematic mirrors and dichroic mirrors, the lasers could be easily redirected to whichever path, and thus the system could also be utilized for red fluorophores and blue opsins.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the system design.

claim: GCaMP6s or GCaMP6f and C1V1-p2A were co-expressed in mouse V1 and excited with 940 nm and 1040 nm light, respectively.
source: We co-expressed GCaMP6s or GCaMP6f (Chen et al., 2013) and C1V1-p2A (Yizhar et al., 2011) in mouse V1 (Figure 1F), and excited them with 940 nm and 1040 nm light, respectively.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup, supported by Figure 1F.

claim: The separation of excitation spectra allowed for minimal cross-talk between the imaging and photostimulation paths.
source: The separation of their excitation spectrum allowed for minimal cross-talk between the imaging and photostimulation paths (Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference about the benefit of the spectral separation, with further discussion referenced.

claim: C1V1-expressed cells were identified through a co-expressed mCherry fluorophore.
source: C1V1-expressed cells were identified through a co-expressed mCherry fluorophore.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying cells expressing the opsin.

claim: Single spikes can be evoked with very low average laser power (~2.25 mW with 20 ms spiral, or ~ 4.5 mW with 10 ms spiral, 1 MHz pulse train, layer 2/3 in vivo).
source: Single spikes can be evoked with very low average laser power (~2.25 mW with 20 ms spiral, or ~ 4.5 mW with 10 ms spiral, 1 MHz pulse train, layer 2/3 in vivo, Figure 1G), latency and jitter (17.0 ± 4.2/8.5 ± 1.6 ms latency, and 2.0±1.5/0.5±0.3 ms jitter for the two conditions, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; jitter defined as the standard deviation of the latency).
evidence: This describes experimental results on spike evocation, supported by Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Single spike evocation has a latency of 17.0 ± 4.2 ms and jitter of 2.0±1.5 ms for 20 ms spiral stimulation, and latency of 8.5 ± 1.6 ms and jitter of 0.5±0.3 ms for 10 ms spiral stimulation.
source: Single spikes can be evoked with very low average laser power (~2.25 mW with 20 ms spiral, or ~ 4.5 mW with 10 ms spiral, 1 MHz pulse train, layer 2/3 in vivo, Figure 1G), latency and jitter (17.0 ± 4.2/8.5 ± 1.6 ms latency, and 2.0±1.5/0.5±0.3 ms jitter for the two conditions, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; jitter defined as the standard deviation of the latency).
evidence: This describes experimental measurements of spike timing, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: With a higher power (10 ~ 20 mW), neural activity could also be evoked with photostimulation duration as short as 1 ms.
source: With a higher power (10 ~ 20 mW), neural activity could also be evoked with photostimulation duration as short as 1 ms (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes experimental results on short-duration stimulation, supported by Figure 2.

claim: Compared with alternative scanless strategies like temporal focusing or pure holographic approaches, the hybrid approach is simple, accommodates large numbers of simultaneous targets, and appears to have a better power budget for large population photostimulation in general.
source: Compared with alternative scanless strategy like temporal focusing (Rickgauer et al., 2014; Mardinly et al., 2017; Hernandez et al., 2016; Pégard et al., 2017) or pure holographic approaches (Dal Maschio et al., 2017), where the laser power is distributed across the whole cell body of each targeted neuron, our hybrid approach is simple, accommodates large numbers of simultaneous targets, and appears to have a better power budget for large population photostimulation in general.
evidence: This is a comparison of the hybrid approach to alternative methods, supported by citations and data in the manuscript.

claim: When photostimulation duration was above 5 ms, the hybrid approach required about half of the laser power than the scanless approach to evoke similar response in the neuron.
source: On our system, when photostimulation duration was above 5 ms, the hybrid approach required about half of the laser power than the scanless approach to evoke similar response in the neuron; at 1 ms photostimulation duration, the hybrid approach shows a trend with smaller power budget (but not significant, p=0.17 using one-way ANOVA test) than the scanless approach (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes experimental comparison results, supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 1 ms photostimulation duration, the hybrid approach shows a trend with smaller power budget (but not significant, p=0.17 using one-way ANOVA test) than the scanless approach.
source: On our system, when photostimulation duration was above 5 ms, the hybrid approach required about half of the laser power than the scanless approach to evoke similar response in the neuron; at 1 ms photostimulation duration, the hybrid approach shows a trend with smaller power budget (but not significant, p=0.17 using one-way ANOVA test) than the scanless approach (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes experimental comparison results with statistical analysis, supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The scanless approach employs a spatial multiplexed strategy, where the two-photon light is spatially distributed across the entire cell body; to maintain the two-photon excitation efficiency (squared-intensity) within its coverage area, a larger total power is typically required.
source: One reason for this difference is that the scanless approach employs a spatial multiplexed strategy, where the two-photon light is spatially distributed across the entire cell body; to maintain the two-photon excitation efficiency (squared-intensity) within its coverage area, a larger total power is typically required.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the physics of two-photon excitation.

claim: The hybrid approach is a combination of spatial (across different cells) and temporal (within individual cell) multiplexed strategy.
source: The hybrid approach, on the other hand, is a combination of spatial (across different cells) and temporal (within individual cell) multiplexed strategy.
evidence: This describes the nature of the hybrid approach.

claim: The opsin typically has a long opsin decay constant (10 s of millisecond) and this favors the hybrid approach because the opsin channels can stay open during the entire (multiple) spiral scans.
source: While optimal strategy will depend on opsin photophysics, the opsin typically has a long opsin decay constant (Mattis et al., 2011) (10 s of millisecond) and this favors the hybrid approach because the opsin channels can stay open during the entire (multiple) spiral scans.
evidence: This is an explanation based on opsin properties, supported by a citation.

claim: At very short duration, the limited number of laser pulses per unit area may contribute to an efficiency drop of the hybrid approach versus scanless approach.
source: But at very short duration, the limited number of laser pulses per unit area may contribute to an efficiency drop of the hybrid approach versus scanless approach.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the hybrid approach at short durations.

claim: Selected groups of pyramidal cells were targeted and photoactivated throughout three axial depths of layer 2/3 of V1 in anesthetized mice, while simultaneously monitoring neuronal activity in those three planes (240 × 240 μm2 FOV for each plane) at 6.67 vol/s.
source: We tested our 3D all-optical system by targeting and photoactivating selected groups of pyramidal cells throughout three axial depths of layer 2/3 of V1 in anesthetized mice, while simultaneously monitoring neuronal activity in those three planes (240 × 240 μm2 FOV for each plane) at 6.67 vol/s.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and parameters.

claim: Neurons were photoactivated one at a time or as groups/ensembles (M neurons simultaneously, M = 3 ~ 27).
source: Neurons were photoactivated one at a time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), or as groups/ensembles (M neurons simultaneously, M = 3 ~ 27, Figure 3) and the majority of the targeted cells (86 ± 6%, Materials and Methods) showed clear calcium transients in response to the photostimulation (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions, supported by Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of the targeted cells (86 ± 6%) showed clear calcium transients in response to the photostimulation.
source: Neurons were photoactivated one at a time (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), or as groups/ensembles (M neurons simultaneously, M = 3 ~ 27, Figure 3) and the majority of the targeted cells (86 ± 6%, Materials and Methods) showed clear calcium transients in response to the photostimulation (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This describes experimental results, supported by Figure 3C-E.

claim: 8 ~ 11 trials were performed for each stimulation pattern.
source: We performed 8 ~ 11 trials for each stimulation pattern.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: As the simultaneously stimulated neurons number M increased, the response rate for both individual cells and ensembles remained high (both is 82 ± 9%, over all seven stimulation conditions).
source: As the simulatenously stimulated neurons number M increased, the response rate for both individual cells and ensembles remained high (both is 82 ± 9%, over all seven stimulation conditions).
evidence: This describes experimental results on response reliability.

claim: Occasional activity in non-targeted cells (nonspecific activation) was observed during photostimulation.
source: Although we had high targeting accuracy and reliability for exciting targeted cells, we also observed occasional activity in non-targeted cells (nonspecific activation) during photostimulation (Figure 3H).
evidence: This describes an observation from the experiments, supported by Figure 3H.

claim: Nonspecific activation was distance-dependent, and as the distance d between the non-targeted cells and their nearest targeted cells decreased, their probability of activation increased.
source: This was distance-dependent, and as the distance d between the non-targeted cells and their nearest targeted cells decreased, their probability of activation increased (Figure 3H).
evidence: This describes experimental results on nonspecific activation, supported by Figure 3H.

claim: For the same distance d, the probability of nonspecific activation increased with M (number of simultaneously stimulated neurons).
source: And, for the same d, this probability increased with M.
evidence: This describes experimental results on nonspecific activation.

claim: The activation of the non-targeted cells may occur through different mechanisms, such as by direct stimulation (depolarization) of the cells through their neurites that course through the photostimulation region, or through synaptic activation by targeted cells, or by a combination of the two.
source: The activation of the non-targeted cells may occur through different mechanisms, such as by direct stimulation (depolarization) of the cells through their neurites that course through the photostimulation region, or through synaptic activation by targeted cells, or by a combination of the two.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms underlying nonspecific activation.

claim: In experiments with extremely long stimulation durations (480 ~ 962 ms), the nonspecific activation was confined (half response rate) within d < 25 μm in all conditions (M = 3 ~ 27 across three planes spanning a volume of 240 × 240 × 100 μm3).
source: In these experiments, we specifically used extremely long stimulation durations (480 ~ 962 ms) to maximally emulate an undesirable photostimulation scenario. The nonspecific activation was confined (half response rate) within d < 25 μm in all conditions (M = 3 ~ 27 across three planes spanning a volume of 240 × 240 × 100 μm3).
evidence: This describes experimental results on the spatial extent of nonspecific activation.

claim: Nonspecific activation could be reduced by increasing excitation NA, using somatic-restricted expression, as well as sparse expression.
source: Nonspecific activation could be reduced by increasing excitation NA (which is currently limited by the relatively small size of the activation galvanometer mirrors), using somatic-restricted expression (Pégard et al., 2017; Baker et al., 2016; Shemesh et al., 2017), as well as sparse expression.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential strategies to reduce nonspecific activation, supported by citations.

claim: With the low-repetition-rate laser and hybrid scanning strategy, the laser beam can be heavily spatially multiplexed to address a large amount of cells while maintaining a low average power.
source: We then aimed to modulate relatively large groups of neurons in 3D. With the low-repetition-rate laser and hybrid scanning strategy (Discussion), the laser beam can be heavily spatially multiplexed to address a large amount of cells while maintaining a low average power.
evidence: This describes the capability of the system.

claim: Photostimulation of 83 cells across an imaged volume of 480 × 480×150 μm3 in layer 2/3 of V1 in awake mice was performed.
source: We performed photostimulation of 83 cells across an imaged volume of 480 × 480×150 μm3 in layer 2/3 of V1 in awake mice (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes an experimental result, supported by Figure 4.

claim: With a total power of 300 mW and an activation time of ~ 95 ms, more than 50 cells were able to be activated.
source: With a total power of 300 mW and an activation time of ~ 95 ms, we were able to activate more than 50 cells.
evidence: This describes experimental results on large-scale photostimulation.

claim: In one experiment, target cells were sorted into two groups (40 and 43 cells respectively) and photostimulated separately, with more than 30 cells in each group successfully activated simultaneously with clear evoked calcium transient.
source: In one experiment, we further sorted target cells into two groups (40 and 43 cells respectively) and photostimulated them separately. More than 30 cells in each group were successfully activated simultaneously with clear evoked calcium transient.
evidence: This describes experimental results on group-specific photostimulation.

claim: In another example, more than 35 cells out of a target group of 50 cells responded.
source: In another example, more than 35 cells out of a target group of 50 cells responded (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes experimental results, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Large scale photostimulations (>=40 target cells) show that 78 ± 7% of cells in the target ensemble can be successfully activated (excluding cells that never respond in any of the tested photostimulation pattern, 8 ± 3%).
source: These large scale photostimulations (>=40 target cells; Figure 4), show that 78 ± 7% of cells in the target ensemble can be successfully activated (excluding cells that never respond in any of the tested photostimulation pattern, 8 ± 3%, see Materials and Methods).
evidence: This describes experimental results on activation success rate, supported by Figure 4.

claim: Nonspecific photoactivation was more frequent for cells surrounded by target cells, but overall it was confined within 20 μm from the nearest target cell.
source: Nonspecific photoactivation was more frequent for cells surrounded by target cells, but overall it was confined within 20 μm from the nearest target cell (Figure 4F).
evidence: This describes experimental results on nonspecific activation, supported by Figure 4F.

claim: Cells that could be photoactivated individually or in a small ensemble may not get photoactivated when the number of target neurons increases.
source: We also noted that cells that could be photoactivated individually or in a small ensemble may not get photoactivated when the number of target neurons increases.
evidence: This describes an observation from the experiments.

claim: The failure of some cells to be photoactivated in large ensembles could be due to feed forward inhibition, as targeted pyramidal neurons may activate local interneurons, which then could suppress the firing of neighboring cells.
source: We hypothesize that this could be due to feed forward inhibition, as targeted pyramidal neurons may activate local interneurons, which then could suppress the firing of neighboring cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observation.

claim: Nonspecific excitation can be minimized with sparse stimulation, by simply reducing the likelihood of stimulating directly adjacent cells.
source: Nonspecific excitation can be minimized with sparse stimulation, by simply reducing the likelihood of stimulating directly adjacent cells.
evidence: This is an inference about how to minimize nonspecific excitation.

claim: One naturally sparse pool of cells are cortical interneurons.
source: One naturally sparse pool of cells are cortical interneurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical anatomy.

claim: Different interneuron classes participate in cortical microcircuits that could serve as gateways for information processing.
source: Different interneuron classes participate in cortical microcircuits that could serve as gateways for information processing (Muñoz et al., 2017; Karnani et al., 2014).

claim: Interneurons are located sparsely in the cortex, yet are highly connected to excitatory populations.
source: These interneurons are located sparsely in the cortex, yet are highly connected to excitatory populations (Fino and Yuste, 2011), and are known to strongly modulate cortical activity (Tsumoto et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Interneurons are known to strongly modulate cortical activity.
source: These interneurons are located sparsely in the cortex, yet are highly connected to excitatory populations (Fino and Yuste, 2011), and are known to strongly modulate cortical activity (Tsumoto et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The effect of simultaneous stimulation of selective subset of interneurons with single cell resolution has not been studied in detail, as previous reports have largely relied on one-photon optogenetics where widespread activation is the norm.
source: However, the effect of simultaneous stimulation of selective subset of interneurons with single cell resolution has not been studied in detail, as previous reports have largely relied on one-photon optogenetics where widespread activation is the norm (Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012) [but see Ref. (Karnani et al., 2016) for single cell interneuron stimulations].
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, supported by citations.

claim: The all-optical approach was used to examine the effect of photoactivating specific sets of interneurons in 3D on the activity of pyramidal cells that responded to visual stimuli in awake head-fixed mice.
source: To explore this, we used our all-optical approach to examine the effect of photoactivating specific sets of interneurons in 3D on the activity of pyramidal cells that responded to visual stimuli in awake head-fixed mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach, supported by Figure 5.

claim: Cre-dependent C1V1 was expressed in somatostatin (SOM) inhibitory interneurons (SOM-Cre mice), while simultaneously also expressing GCaMP6s in both pyramidal cells and interneurons, in layer 2/3 of mouse V1.
source: Using viral vectors, we expressed Cre-dependent C1V1 in somatostatin (SOM) inhibitory interneurons (SOM-Cre mice), while simultaneously also expressing GCaMP6s in both pyramidal cells and interneurons, in layer 2/3 of mouse V1.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The responses of pyramidal cells across three planes (separated by ~ 45 μm each) to orthogonal visual stimuli consisting of drifting grating without photostimulation were first imaged.
source: We first imaged the responses of pyramidal cells across three planes (separated by ~ 45 μm each) to orthogonal visual stimuli consisting of drifting grating without photostimulation.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: A group of SOM cells (M = 9, with seven showing responses) across three planes were simultaneously photostimulated concurrently with the visual stimuli.
source: We then simultaneously photostimulated a group of SOM cells (M = 9, with seven showing responses) across these three planes concurrently with the visual stimuli (Figure 5A–C; Materials and Methods).

claim: The orientation selectivity of highly selective cells was largely abolished by SOM cell photoactivation.
source: Moreover, the orientation selectivity of highly selective cells was largely abolished by SOM cell photoactivation (Figure 5E).

claim: The observation that SOM cells inhibit nearby pyramidal cells is consistent with reports using one-photon optogenetics in vivo or with two-photon glutamate uncaging in vitro.
source: This is consistent with reports that SOM cells inhibit nearby pyramidal cells with one-photon optogenetics in vivo (Lee et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012) or with two-photon glutamate uncaging in vitro (Fino and Yuste, 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The two-photon approach provides high precision 3D manipulation over groups of cells and simultaneous readout of neuronal activity across the network in vivo.
source: Our two-photon approach provides high precision 3D manipulation over groups of cells (Figure 5D), and simultaneous readout of neuronal activity across the network in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the approach, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: The approach could be useful for dissecting the excitatory and inhibitory interactions in cortical circuits in vivo.
source: Thus, our approach could be useful for dissecting the excitatory and inhibitory interactions in cortical circuits in vivo.

claim: The 3D all-optical method could be used to map the functional connectivity of neural circuits and probe the causal relationships between the activity of neuronal ensembles and behavior.
source: We describe here a 3D all-optical method that could be used to map the functional connectivity of neural circuits and probe the causal relationships between the activity of neuronal ensembles and behavior.

claim: The method extends previous in vivo methods from planar to volumetric targeting, and increases the total number of cells that could be simultaneously photoactivated.
source: We extend previous in vivo methods from planar to volumetric targeting, and increase the total number of cells that could be simultaneously photoactivated.
evidence: This is a statement about the advances made by the method.

claim: This represents a significant advance of precision optogenetics towards large spatial scales and volumes.
source: This represents a significant advance of precision optogenetics towards large spatial scales and volumes.

claim: The dual beam path microscope facilitates independent control of imaging and photostimulation lasers, and is thus well suited for controlling and detecting neural activity, without any disturbing or slow movements of the objective.
source: The dual beam path microscope facilitates independent control of imaging and photostimulation lasers, and is thus well suited for controlling and detecting neural activity, without any disturbing or slow movements of the objective.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the microscope design.

claim: To simultaneously photostimulate multiple cells with two-photon excitation, it is becoming common to use holographic approaches.
source: To simultaneously photostimulate multiple cells with two-photon excitation, it is becoming common to use holographic approaches (Nikolenko et al., 2008; Packer et al., 2012; Packer et al., 2015; Dal Maschio et al., 2017; Mardinly et al., 2017; Pégard et al., 2017).

claim: Spatial light modulators can generate an 'arbitrary' 3D pattern on the sample, limited only by Maxwell's equations, and the space-bandwidth product of the modulation device.
source: Spatial light modulators can generate an 'arbitrary' 3D pattern on the sample, limited only by Maxwell's equations, and the space-bandwidth product of the modulation device.

claim: With SLMs, one can independently target a very large number of sites, far in excess of what is demonstrated in the manuscript, but the number of addressable neurons is limited by the allowable power budget.
source: With SLMs, one can independently target a very large number of sites, far in excess of what we demonstrate here, but the number of addressable neurons is limited by the allowable power budget.

claim: Special care has to be taken to minimize the total power deposited on the brain, and avoid direct and indirect thermal effects.

claim: The issue of power budget was addressed by using a hybrid holographic strategy and a low-repetition-rate laser for photostimulation, with high peak intensities for efficient two-photon excitation, but moderate average power.
source: We addressed this issue by using a hybrid holographic strategy and a low-repetition-rate laser for photostimulation, with high peak intensities for efficient two-photon excitation, but moderate average power.

claim: The approach allowed targeting a large group of cells with low average power (e.g. 83 targeted cells across an imaged volume of 480 × 480 × 150 μm3 in awake mice V1 layer 2/3 with 300 mW in total).

claim: As cells generally are not targeted continuously, no heat induced effects on cell health are expected under the stimulation conditions.
source: As these cells generally are not targeted continuously, we do not expect any heat induced effects on cell health under our stimulation conditions (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).

claim: In the hybrid strategy, a group of beamlets is generated by the SLM that target the centroids of the desired neurons.
source: In our hybrid strategy, a group of beamlets is generated by the SLM that target the centroids of the desired neurons.
evidence: This describes the hybrid strategy.

claim: Each discrete focal point in the hologram maintains sufficient axial confinement for typical inter-cell spacing.
source: Each discrete focal point in the hologram maintains sufficient axial confinement for typical inter-cell spacing.

claim: The beamlets are then rapidly spirally scanned over the neurons' cell bodies by post-SLM galvanometers.
source: These beamlets are then rapidly spirally scanned over the neurons' cell bodies by post-SLM galvanometers.
evidence: This describes the hybrid strategy.

claim: The full 3D hologram has a decreased axial resolution as its lateral extend increases.
source: Though simplest, the full 3D hologram has a decreased axial resolution as its lateral extend increases (Papagiakoumou et al., 2008), and is subject to light contamination to the non-targeted cells, particularly in scattering tissues such as the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of full 3D holograms, supported by a citation.

claim: The full 3D hologram is subject to light contamination to the non-targeted cells, particularly in scattering tissues such as the mammalian brain.
source: Though simplest, the full 3D hologram has a decreased axial resolution as its lateral extend increases (Papagiakoumou et al., 2008), and is subject to light contamination to the non-targeted cells, particularly in scattering tissues such as the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of full 3D holograms.

claim: Temporal focusing decouples axial from lateral extent of the hologram by coupling the holographic pattern to a grating such that only one axial position in the sample has sufficient spectral content to generate a short laser pulse, thus tightening the axial confinement.
source: In contrast, temporal focusing (Oron et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2005) decouples axial from lateral extent of the hologram by coupling the holographic pattern to a grating (Papagiakoumou et al., 2008) such that only one axial position in the sample has sufficient spectral content to generate a short laser pulse, thus tightening the axial confinement.

claim: Recent reports have extended temporal focusing to 3D stimulation.

claim: Scanless approaches require higher laser powers per cell in general than the hybrid method.
source: Regardless of the exact implementation, these scanless approaches require higher laser powers per cell in general than our hybrid method.

claim: It would likely require even more power for the same excitation with temporal focusing, as its tighter axial confinement would excite less of the membrane.
source: It would likely require even more power for the same excitation with temporal focusing, as its tighter axial confinement would excite less of the membrane.

claim: The spiral scan strategy requires a lower laser power budget per cell, and is very scalable towards activating large number of simultaneously targeted cells, making it a practical tool to study ensembles in neural circuits.

claim: One key strategy to lower the total average laser power in patterned photostimulation was to employ a low-repetition-rate laser for photostimulation.

source: The average laser power Pave scales with the product of laser peak power Ppeak and pulse repetition rate frep.

source: Since the laser beam is split into M beamlets to target M individual cell, the two-photon excitation for each cell scales with (Ppeak/M)2 (Denk et al., 1990).

claim: To maintain the required Ppeak for a large M, frep was reduced instead of increasing Pave.
source: To maintain the required Ppeak for a large M, we reduced frep instead of increasing Pave.

claim: The two-photon photostimulation laser used had a low frep (200 kHz ~ 1 MHz), leading to a significant increase in Ppeak and thus the number of possible simultaneously targeted cells M, with the same Pave.

claim: Most opsins open ion channels, the average open time is much longer than the laser's interpulse interval (1/frep), and multiple ions can be conducted during each photostimulation.

claim: Opsins are ideal targets for low-repetition rate, high peak power excitation.
source: Thus opsins are ideal targets for low-repetition rate, high peak power excitation.
